evidence: The graph formulas are exact. Vertex connectivity is n-M=q. In the non-Hamiltonian regime M>q, any cycle uses at most as many vertices of the largest part B as outside it, so length is at most 2q; every q-subset of B alternates with all q vertices outside B to attain 2q, and equality forces precisely those vertex sets. If M<=q, Dirac gives a Hamiltonian cycle. The analogous path inequality allows one extra B vertex and gives the traceability boundary M<=q+1. Pairwise intersections then reduce to the exact intersection range max(0,2k-M)<=t<=k for two k-subsets of an M-set, producing the stated spectra, common core O, and equality regimes for the Smith and Hippchen bounds. Small boundary cases, including M=q and M=q+1, are consistent with the formulas.

evidence: The complete-bipartite sharpness mechanism is prior art and is excluded from the novelty claim. The audited contribution is the full complete-multipartite classification of longest-object vertex sets, common core, entire pairwise intersection spectrum, and equality regimes. Accessible general Smith/Hippchen literature found during the audit discusses general intersection bounds and the bipartite example, not this exact class-wide package. Haidong Wu's 2026 Discrete Applied Mathematics paper has a directly relevant title, but its full text was unavailable via open sources; an authorized Oxford attempt reached a publisher human-verification gate, so it was not claimed as read. The surviving claim is elementary enough that older differently worded class-specific literature remains a meaningful risk, recorded explicitly, but there is no concrete evidence of prior coverage of the exact package.

The result gives a complete, transparent test class for Smith's and Hippchen's conjectured connectivity bounds. Beyond confirming the inequalities, it identifies a common minimum-cut core and all possible pairwise intersection sizes, enlarging the known sharpness family from complete bipartite examples to all relevant complete multipartite graphs. This is a meaningful exact structural result even though the proof is elementary.
